Intro

On runtime during an execution,
Luawl virtualizes your script
at runtime and sends back a
new, uniquely obfuscated build.

Scripts are compiled and run through the
custom Lua VM on a new, non-standard
instruction set built to virtualize each run.

For transparency to privacy,
Luawl is built to be a fully amnesic
a self-attestable obfuscation layer
hardware-isolated enclaves.

Core Features

Protection with a verifiable boundary

Luawl is a runtime obfuscator built around a zero-trust boundary, protected outputs, and independently verifiable handling.

New features, fixes, and improvements

Privacy and transparency

Luawl can now show how a protected program was handled without exposing the program itself. Each valid run produces a verification record with its outcome and status.

Verification does not depend on our dashboard. Review the run record independently without exposing protected details.

Jul 23, 2026

Privacy and transparency

Luawl can now show how a protected program was handled without exposing the program itself. Each valid run produces a verification record with its outcome and status.

Verification does not depend on our dashboard. Review the run record independently without exposing protected details.

Jul 23, 2026

Execution receipts

We rebuilt how Luawl records executions. Every valid run now has a clear verification record you can inspect after completion.

Verification makes handling reviewable without exposing protected details. Requests that do not qualify remain separate from completed runs.

Transparency keeps each execution and its verification record together across the product.

May 14, 2026

Execution receipts

We rebuilt how Luawl records executions. Every valid run now has a clear verification record you can inspect after completion.

Verification makes handling reviewable without exposing protected details. Requests that do not qualify remain separate from completed runs.

Transparency keeps each execution and its verification record together across the product.

May 14, 2026

Loader authorization controls

Projects can now define execution requirements before protected output is returned. Existing access rules stay outside the protected runtime.

Valid executions receive protected output; requests that do not qualify stop before delivery. Records separate attempts from completed runs.

Mar 12, 2026

Loader authorization controls

Projects can now define execution requirements before protected output is returned. Existing access rules stay outside the protected runtime.

Valid executions receive protected output; requests that do not qualify stop before delivery. Records separate attempts from completed runs.

Mar 12, 2026

Protected execution model

Luawl now prepares supported scripts for its protected execution model. The loader is only the entry point; protected output is returned only for a valid execution.

Each valid execution is handled independently, with the details of that handling kept behind the service boundary. Support expands only as behavior preservation is proven.

Broader Lua support will follow as compatibility and behavior-preservation tests are completed.

Jan 20, 2026

FAQ

Answers to the questions that come up most.

Learn how Luawl works, how runtime builds and attestation are handled, and what to expect from every execution.

General

Plans & Billing

Privacy & Transparency

Got Questions?

Need help with a build or deployment? Our team is here to make things easy. Don’t hesitate to reach out.

Email us →

What happens when a loader is executed?

The loader can be run, but only a valid execution receives protected output. Requests that do not qualify stop there.

Does every execution follow the same path?

Each valid execution is handled according to its requirements. Internal handling details are not exposed.

What does the custom Lua VM protect?

The custom Lua VM changes how supported code is handled during an execution, keeping the protected program away from the public interface.

What does the public loader contain?

The public loader is the entry point for an execution. It does not expose the protected program or its internal handling.

How are loader requests authorized?

Projects can define what counts as a valid execution. Requests that do not meet those requirements stop before protected output is returned.

What can I track after deployment?

Projects can track attempts, completed executions, and verification status without exposing the protected program.
